pharm: Acetic-acid-derivative NSAID with anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic activity via prostaglandin synthesis inhibition; relative COX-2 selectivity at usual doses.
quick: Acute pain 200-400 mg q6-8h (max 1000 mg/day); OA/RA 300 mg BID-TID or 400-500 mg BID
Take with food/milk to reduce GI upset
Avoid from ~20 weeks; contraindicated from ~30 weeks
BP, renal function, CBC/Hb, signs of GI bleed, LFTs
summary: Etodolac is an NSAID (relatively COX-2-preferential) for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and acute pain. Like all NSAIDs it carries a BOXED WARNING for increased cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke - and it is contraindicated for peri-CABG pain) and for serious GI bleeding, ulceration, and perforation, which can be fatal and occur without warning. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. It can cause renal impairment, fluid retention/hypertension, and rare severe skin or hepatic reactions, and it raises levels/toxicity of lithium, methotrexate, digoxin, and cyclosporine.
indications: Management of the signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis (acute and long-term)
Management of the signs and symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis (acute and long-term)

dosage.n: Total daily dose up to 1000 mg; doses >1000 mg/day not adequately studied

dosage.d: 300 mg twice or three times daily, OR 400 mg twice daily, OR 500 mg twice daily
dosage.n: Maintenance as low as 600 mg/day may suffice; do not exceed 1000 mg/day; use lowest effective dose

dosage.d: Use with caution; no routine adjustment for mild-moderate impairment
dosage.n: May further reduce renal function; avoid in advanced renal disease

admin: Take with food or milk to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals
Swallow tablets/capsules whole; do not exceed 1000 mg/day
Do not use immediately before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
Reassess need periodically in chronic use; monitor BP, renal function, and for GI symptoms
moa: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, primarily through inhibition of cyclooxygenase (with relative COX-2 preference at therapeutic doses), producing anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects. The active enantiomer is the [+]S-form.

absolute: History of asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reaction to aspirin or other NSAIDs (NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease)
Setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
relative: Active or history of GI ulceration/bleeding
Hypertension, heart failure, or fluid retention
monitor: Hemoglobin/hematocrit and signs of GI bleeding

preg: Avoid NSAIDs from about 20 weeks gestation onward (risk of fetal renal dysfunction and oligohydramnios), and avoid use at about 30 weeks and later (risk of premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus). Limit dose and duration if used between 20 and 30 weeks.
lact: Trace amounts of some NSAIDs appear in human milk; it is unknown whether etodolac is excreted. Because of potential serious adverse effects in the infant, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, weighing maternal need.
renal: Use with caution; like other NSAIDs, etodolac can reduce renal blood flow and further impair function in patients with pre-existing renal impairment, heart failure, hepatic dysfunction, or volume depletion. Generally no dose adjustment for mild-moderate impairment, but avoid in advanced renal disease.
hepatic: Use with caution; rare cases of severe hepatic reactions (jaundice, fatal hepatitis) have occurred with NSAIDs. Monitor liver enzymes with prolonged use and discontinue if liver injury develops.

major: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, heparin, aspirin) - increased bleeding risk
Other NSAIDs/aspirin (additive GI toxicity - avoid combining)
moderate: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers (diminished antihypertensive effect)
Diuretics (reduced natriuretic/antihypertensive effect; 'triple whammy' AKI with ACEi/ARB + diuretic)
minor: Antacids (reduce peak concentration ~15-20% without changing extent of absorption)
interactions.food: Take with food/milk; food can slow absorption rate but absorption is essentially complete.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - increases the risk of GI bleeding.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor renal function, CBC/hemoglobin, blood pressure, and liver enzymes with prolonged therapy; monitor lithium, digoxin, and methotrexate levels when co-administered.

serious: GI bleeding, ulceration, perforation (can be fatal, often without warning)
rare: Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

monitoring: Blood pressure (especially when starting or increasing dose)
Renal function (creatinine, urine output), particularly in at-risk patients
Hemoglobin/hematocrit and signs of GI bleeding in long-term therapy
Signs of fluid retention and heart failure
Lithium, digoxin, and methotrexate levels if co-administered
counsel: Take with food or milk and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed
Stop and seek care for black/tarry stools, vomiting blood, severe stomach pain, or unexpected weight gain/swelling
Seek emergency help for chest pain, weakness on one side, slurred speech, or trouble breathing
Avoid alcohol and other NSAIDs (including aspirin) unless your doctor advises
Tell your doctor about kidney, heart, liver, or blood-pressure problems and any blood thinners
Avoid during the last months of pregnancy
pk: Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light/moisture per labeling
pearls: BOXED WARNING: increased cardiovascular thrombotic events and serious GI bleeding/perforation; contraindicated peri-CABG
Relatively COX-2-preferential at therapeutic doses, which may modestly lower GI toxicity versus non-selective NSAIDs, but GI and CV risks remain
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration; reassess in chronic use
Watch the 'triple whammy' (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) for acute kidney injury
Can falsely elevate urinary bilirubin assays (etodolac metabolites)
Raises lithium, methotrexate, and digoxin levels - monitor closely
missed: If taken on a schedule, take the missed dose as soon as you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume your schedule. Do not double the dose. For as-needed pain dosing, take only when needed.
overdose: Symptoms are usually limited to lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain and are generally reversible with supportive care; GI bleeding, hypertension, acute renal failure, respiratory depression, coma, and anaphylactoid reactions can rarely occur. There is no specific antidote. Manage with symptomatic/supportive care; activated charcoal (60-100 g adults, 1-2 g/kg children) may help within 4 hours of ingestion. Hemodialysis is not useful (high protein binding).
